content: 1. Obie Baizley, DC, was a chiropractor from Manitoba, Canada, who also served as a politician. 2. Fred Barge, DC, authored numerous books on chiropractic, covering topics such as chiropractic philosophy and practice management. He was elected President of the International Chiropractor's Association in 1988. 3. Russell Gibbons, BA, was a historian who wrote extensively about chiropractic and its practitioners. He also founded the journal Chiropractic History. 4. Henri Gillet, DC, practiced chiropractic in Belgium and developed the Motion Palpation technique in response to the Belgian government prohibiting chiropractors from taking X-rays. 5. Clarence Gonstead, DC, was the developer of the Gonstead technique and established the Mt. Horeb Clinic. 6. George Goodheart, DC, was the creator of Applied Kinesiology and served as the first chiropractor for the U.S. Olympic Team. 7. Gerry E. Hinton, DC, was a chiropractor who also served as a Louisiana State Senator. 8. Earl Homewood, DC, was the President of the Canadian Memorial Chiropractic College (CMCC) and authored the book Neurodynamics of Vertebral Subluxation. 9. Fred Illi, a Swiss chiropractor, was a pioneering chiropractic researcher in the early 20th century. He developed theories on spinal biomechanics and collaborated with Joseph Janse at the National College in Chicago. 10. Teddy Infuhr, DC, was a chiropractor who had previously gained fame as a child actor. 11. William Ivens, DC, was a chiropractor who also served as a member of the Manitoba Legislature in Canada. 12. Joseph Janse, DC, was instrumental in founding the independently chartered Council on Chiropractic Education (CCE). As President of the National College (now National University of Health Sciences), he led the institution to become the first chiropractic college to achieve federal recognition. He was also a renowned anatomist and established the Journal of Manipulative and Physiological Therapeutics. 13. Bernard Jensen, DC, was the inventor of the controversial diagnostic method known as Iridology. 14. Joseph C. Keating, Jr., PhD (1950–2007), was a clinical psychologist who dedicated his career to teaching and researching chiropractic. He is best known for his extensive publications as a historian of the chiropractic profession. 15. He also founded and served as the first president of Logan College of Chiropractic. 16. Thomas Robert Mason, DC, was a chiropractor who also worked as an actor. 17. Volney Mathison, DC, was an inventor. 18. Bartlett Joshua (B.J.) Palmer, DC, the son of chiropractic founder D.D. Palmer, played a pivotal role in advancing chiropractic as a profession. He assumed leadership of the Palmer School of Chiropractic in 1904 and contributed to research, spinal adjustment techniques, and raising educational standards. He also worked to overcome legal and financial challenges to secure chiropractic's place in the health sciences. 19. Daniel David (D.D.) Palmer, DC, is recognized as the founder of modern chiropractic in the late 19th century. He theorized that the body’s natural healing ability relied on proper nervous system function, which could be disrupted by spinal misalignments (vertebral subluxations). He performed his first chiropractic adjustments in 1895, reportedly curing a man of deafness and another of heart trouble. In 1897, he established the Palmer Infirmary and Cure, which later became the Palmer School of Chiropractic. 20. David D. Palmer, DC, the grandson of D.D. Palmer, became president of the Palmer School in 1961. He modernized the institution, renamed it Palmer College of Chiropractic, and achieved non-profit status for the college. Under his leadership, the college gained accreditation from the Council on Chiropractic Education and the North Central Association of Colleges and Schools. 21. Mabel Heath Palmer, DC, was the first woman in chiropractic and a significant influence on her husband, B.J. Palmer. She became a chiropractor in 1905, was a recognized authority on anatomy, and taught at the Palmer School for over 30 years. She was a trusted advisor to her husband in all aspects of the chiropractic profession. 22. Jim Parker, DC, was the founder of Parker College of Chiropractic in Texas. 23. John Lyle Robinson, DC, was a chiropractor who also served as a member of the Canadian Parliament. 24. Walter Wardwell, PhD (1917–2005), was a sociologist and historian who extensively studied and wrote about chiropractic. His works include the definitive history Chiropractic: History and Evolution of a New Profession and numerous articles on the profession’s social and historical aspects. 25. Clarence Weiant, DC, PhD, was the first chiropractor to also earn a PhD (in anthropology). He worked at the Chiropractic Institute of New York (CINY) and published scientifically rigorous research supporting chiropractic, making him a prominent advocate for the profession. 26. John Wolfe, Sr., DC, was a graduate of Palmer College of Chiropractic and the founder of Northwestern Health Sciences University in 1941. He served as the university’s president for over 40 years, overseeing its chiropractic college and its rigorous basic sciences curriculum.
